sections.title: From Single Cell to Enterprise Scale
learningObjectives: Understand the shift in thinking from single-cell to multi-plant deployment
Know that this module covers the enterprise-scale thinking that completes the track
sections.content: Earlier L4A modules addressed designing and integrating a MoRo cell within one facility. This module addresses what changes when that thinking scales to multiple plants, larger fleets, and enterprise-level infrastructure decisions - the kind of conversation a Systems Engineer has with leadership when a single successful deployment becomes a multi-site rollout.

sections.title: Architecture Patterns for Scale
learningObjectives: Understand general architectural considerations that change at multi-plant scale
Recognize the difference between a pattern that works for one cell and one that scales
sections.content: An architecture decision that works cleanly for a single cell - a specific network topology, a particular integration approach - doesn't automatically scale to ten plants. Multi-site architecture needs to account for consistency (so each site doesn't become a bespoke system requiring separate expertise), while still allowing for genuine site-specific variation where it's actually necessary. This module covers the thinking behind that balance, not a fixed template, since every enterprise rollout differs.

sections.title: Network and Infrastructure at Scale
learningObjectives: Understand how network and infrastructure considerations change across multiple sites
Recognize centralized versus distributed infrastructure trade-offs
sections.content: At multi-plant scale, questions arise that don't exist at single-site scale: should fleet data be centralized (one system monitoring all sites) or distributed (each site largely independent, with centralized reporting only)? Each approach has trade-offs in reliability, latency, and administrative overhead. Specific recommendations depend heavily on DiFacto's actual infrastructure and client context, which this module will reference once multi-plant case examples are available.

keyTerms.note: One system monitoring and managing all sites from a single place.
Each site largely runs independently, with only reporting shared centrally.

sections.title: Standardization Versus Customization
learningObjectives: Understand the trade-off between standardized rollout and site-specific customization
Recognize how this decision affects long-term maintainability
sections.content: A fully standardized rollout (identical configuration everywhere) is easier to maintain and train for, but may not fit every site's specific layout or workflow. Full customization fits each site better initially, but creates long-term maintenance burden as each site diverges. The Systems Engineer's role in a multi-plant rollout often involves finding where standardization genuinely serves the business versus where site-specific accommodation is worth the added complexity.

keyTerms.note: Using the same configuration at every site so it is easier to maintain and train for.

video.title: Standardize or customize in 30 seconds
video.transcript: Standardize or customize? In 30 seconds. Fully standardized: identical everywhere. Easier to maintain and train for. But it may not fit every site. Full customization fits each site better. But sites diverge: a long-term maintenance burden. Standardize where it serves; adapt where it is worth it.

sections.title: ROI Modeling for Scale Decisions
learningObjectives: Understand the basic components of an ROI case for multi-plant deployment
Recognize how this connects to the throughput and payback projections made when a deployment is proposed
sections.content: Scaling decisions need an economic case, not just a technical one - factoring in deployment cost per site, expected throughput improvement, reduced labor dependency, and payback timeline. This connects to the projected throughput and payback figures quoted when a deployment is first proposed - as a Systems Engineer, you may be the person checking that those projections hold up against actual deployment data once a rollout is underway.

keyTerms.note: Economic analysis of deployment cost against expected returns (throughput, reduced labor dependency) to justify and validate a scaling decision.
How long a deployment takes to earn back its cost.

sections.title: Completing the Systems Engineer Track
learningObjectives: Understand how this module completes the L4A curriculum
Recognize the path forward into L4B or L5
sections.content: This module completes the L4A Systems Engineer curriculum, building on cell-level design and integration (earlier modules) with the enterprise-scale thinking needed for larger rollouts. From here, certified Systems Engineers may progress toward L4B (Advanced Programming) for deeper technical implementation work, or toward L5 (Master Instructor) if their path moves toward training other MoRo users.

questions.question: A rollout team proposes an identical configuration at every site. According to the lesson, what is the drawback?
options: It may not fit every site's specific layout or workflow
It is harder to maintain and train for
It makes sites diverge over time
questions.feedback: Correct. Full standardization is easier to maintain and train for, but may not fit every site.

questions.question: A network topology worked cleanly in one cell. Leadership wants it copied to ten plants. What does the lesson say a multi-site architecture must account for?
options: An identical configuration everywhere, with no exceptions
Consistency across sites, while still allowing site-specific variation where it is actually necessary
A separate bespoke design for each site
questions.feedback: Correct. What works at single-cell scale doesn't automatically transfer to enterprise scale.

questions.question: Which describes distributed infrastructure, as this lesson defines it?
options: One system monitors and manages all sites from a single place
Each site runs largely independently, with centralized reporting only
Each site uses a different robot model
questions.feedback: Correct. In a distributed setup each site is largely independent, with centralized reporting only. Each approach has trade-offs in reliability, latency, and administrative overhead.

questions.question: What is the risk of full site-specific customization across a multi-plant rollout?
options: Safety standards no longer apply to sites that have been customized
Training becomes unnecessary because every site is unique to itself
Heavy long-term maintenance as sites drift apart
questions.feedback: Correct. Full customization fits each site better initially but creates maintenance burden over time.

questions.question: What role might a Systems Engineer play regarding the ROI projections made when a deployment is proposed?
options: Setting the price each customer pays for the deployment, based on the plant's size
Checking that the projections hold up against actual deployment data
Writing the sales proposal before any technical review
questions.feedback: Correct. Systems Engineers may validate real-world performance against the economic case made when a deployment was proposed.
